title: Determinants of the Nucleocytoplasmic Balance of the Cucumber Mosaic Virus and Peanut Stunt Virus 2b Proteins Regulate the Subcellular Localization and RNA Silencing Suppressor Activity.
abstract: The 2b protein of cucumoviruses is an RNA silencing suppressor (RSS), and its activity is associated with its nucleocytoplasmic localization. However, the contribution of nuclear localization signals (NLSs), nuclear export signals (NESs), and their sequence context remains poorly understood. Here, we compare cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) and peanut stunt virus (PSV) 2b proteins and their NLS- and NES-containing regions using recombinant proteins. The subcellular localization of PSV 2b has not been characterized, and no protein structural model has been reported previously. CMV 2b displayed a balanced nucleocytoplasmic distribution and strong RSS activity, whereas PSV 2b showed predominantly nuclear localization and weaker RSS activity. Exchange of the N-terminal region and NLSs resulted in pronounced changes in localization and RSS activity. PPC 2b, containing the CMV C-terminal region preceded by PSV sequence, showed the highest RSS activity, while the corresponding recombinant virus caused the most severe symptoms. AlphaFold analysis demonstrated lower structural confidence and higher predicted flexibility in the NES-containing C-terminal regions of CMV 2b and PPC 2b, compared with PSV 2b and CCP 2b, containing the PSV C-terminal region preceded by CMV sequence. These differences may influence NES accessibility and nuclear export.

title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
abstract: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.

title: Phylogeny of Termites Inferred from Mitogenomic Data with a Large Taxon Sampling.
abstract: Background: Termites (epifamily Termitoidae) represent the oldest known lineage of eusocial insects, yet their higher-level phylogenetic relationships remain contentious. Methods: We sequenced ten new termite mitochondrial genomes (mitogenomes) from Australia and China and integrated them with published data to assemble a comprehensive dataset of 560 species, including 553 termite ingroup species representing all 13 extant families and seven Cryptocercus outgroups. Phylogenetic relationships were inferred using maximum likelihood analyses of mitochondrial protein-coding genes and ribosomal RNA genes under amino acid and nucleotide datasets. Results: All newly sequenced mitogenomes contained the canonical set of 37 mitochondrial genes, exhibited a pronounced A+T bias, and retained the ancestral insect gene order. Mastotermes darwiniensis (Mastotermitidae) was consistently recovered as the sister lineage to all other termites. Among the basal lineages, the relationship ((Hodotermopsidae + Stolotermitidae) + (Archotermopsidae + Hodotermitidae)) received strong support. Kalotermitidae was recovered as monophyletic and as the sister group to Neoisoptera. The traditional Rhinotermitidae was non-monophyletic, and the analyses supported the revised family-level classification that restricts Rhinotermitidae to Rhinotermitinae while recognizing Psammotermitidae, Termitogetonidae, and Heterotermitidae as separate lineages. Within Termitidae, Macrotermitinae was recovered as the sister group to the remaining termitid lineages, whereas Sphaerotermitinae formed a distinct lineage, consistent with its recognition as a separate subfamily. Conclusions: Our results substantially expand mitogenomic sampling across termites and provide further support for recent family- and subfamily-level taxonomic revisions. The inferred relationships broadly agree with recent molecular studies, while some unresolved relationships require denser taxon sampling and nuclear genomic data.

title: Genetic Diversity of Rose Rosette Virus Isolates in Oklahoma Reveals a Distinct Evolutionary Lineage.
abstract: Rose rosette virus (RRV), a member of the genus Emaravirus, is responsible for rose rosette disease (RRD), which has significant impacts on the rose industry and ornamental landscapes across the United States (US). To better understand the genetic diversity and population structure of RRV, infected rose leaf samples were collected from garden centers, nurseries, retail stores, and wild rose populations. Total RNA was extracted and analyzed using Sanger sequencing and Illumina-based high-throughput sequencing (HTS), resulting in nearly complete genome sequences of 17 RRV isolates. Phylogenetic and population genetic analyses incorporating >100 publicly available RRV isolates revealed a genetically differentiated lineage comprising eight isolates, seven of which were characterized in this study. This lineage, designated the OK Clade, was consistently supported across the concatenated coding-sequence dataset and several individual genomic segments of RRV. Evolutionary modeling estimated that the divergence between the OK Clade and all other RRV isolates likely occurred more than a century ago. Population genetic analyses further supported substantial differentiation between the OK Clade and other RRV isolates. RRV exhibited greater nucleotide diversity than previously reported, indicating that the genetic diversity of the virus may be broader than previously recognized. Potential recombination breakpoints were also identified in RNA1 and RNA5, although additional analyses are required to validate these events. Collectively, these findings identify a geographically associated and genetically distinct RRV lineage in Oklahoma and provide new insights into the population structure and evolutionary diversity of RRV.

title: Elucidating the Evolutionary History of the Critically Endangered Batagur baska Using Complete Mitogenome.
abstract: Background/Objectives:Batagur baska is a critically endangered turtle, primarily found in the estuaries and tidal regions of large rivers. B. baska has experienced extensive population declines across most of its range, with no confirmed wild populations remaining. This study aims to generate and characterize a complete mitogenome of B. baska, as well as assess its phylogeny and evolutionary history Methods: Eight mitochondrial genome were generated using next-generation sequencing (NGS). The dataset was used to assess phylogenetic position using Bayesian and Maximum Likelihood approaches, as well as to estimate divergence times. Results: The assembled mitogenomes (16,731, 16,715, 16,662, 16,654, 16,642, 16,582, 16,540, 16,527 bp) comprises 37 genes, including 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 22 transfer RNA genes, and two ribosomal RNA genes, along with a fully resolved non-coding control region. The genome exhibits a typical vertebrate organization with a nucleotide composition heavily biased toward A + T content, consistent with other Geoemydidae turtles. This mitochondrial genome data is combined with existing genetic information to evaluate the species' phylogenetic position. The Bayesian and Maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis confirmed a close genetic relationship between B. baska and B. affinis. Divergence time estimation analyses indicated that the lineage leading to B. baska diverged at approximately 9.12 million years ago (Ma) (95% HPD: 5.11-13.24 Ma), supporting a Miocene origin. Comparative analyses of the newly generated and previously published mitogenomes identified nucleotide variation, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitutions, and indels, present new mitogenome variation not known before. Conclusions: The research provides a complete mitochondrial genome for the species, offering robust phylogenetic and divergence time estimates. This mitogenomic resource also provides a baseline for future population levels which is required to guide potential breeding programs and reintroduction efforts, as well as for long-term monitoring.

title: In situ multimodal imaging reveals compartmentalization of reovirus replication factories.
abstract: Avian reovirus (ARV) belongs to Reoviridae family of viruses with segmented dsRNA genomes. ARV is responsible for significant economic losses to the poultry industry by causing tenosynovitis and chronic respiratory disease in chickens. ARV virion exhibits an outer protein shell enclosing an inner core, which contains 10 unique dsRNA segments and multiple copies of viral polymerase. ARV assembly takes place in so-called viral factories (VFs). They are cytoplasmic membrane-less inclusions, which accumulate viral proteins and RNA and assist capsid assembly, genome packaging and replication. VFs also provide protection from the host cell defence mechanisms by sequestering viral RNA. Given the dense nature of VFs, little is known about ARV assembly and packaging intermediates. To determine the architecture of VFs across the different length scales and infection course, we employed a wide range of imaging methods. Our data reveal that spherical and fluid VF enriched in viral protein σNS become surrounded by σNS-depleted solid-like compartments at late stages of infection. We demonstrate that confocal Raman microscopy allows label-free imaging of VF composition. Volume electron microscopy, along with electron tomography (ET) and in situ cryo-ET, revealed that the inner phase of VF concentrates viral non-structural proteins and assists assembly of viral cores. The larger, RNA-filled and double-layered particles are assembled at the periphery of the inner fluid phase of VF, forming ordered virion arrays. This suggests that ARV VFs are functionally compartmentalized: the inner fluid phase assists RNA assortment and core particle assembly, whereas the peripheral phase is the site of RNA replication inside viral cores and virion completion.

title: Regulation of miR-219 and its target RalGPS is essential for synaptic plasticity at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
abstract: RNA regulatory mechanisms mediate adaptive responses relying on rapid changes in gene expression. By examining microRNA (miRNA)-mediated control of structural synaptic plasticity, we find miR-219 and five other conserved miRNAs regulate activity-induced morphogenesis at Drosophila glutamatergic synapses. Among miRNA targets downregulated by acute stimulation, the Ral activating factor RalGPS is necessary for presynaptic morphogenesis and is sufficient to block plasticity. We find that RalGPS must be held within a narrow range of expression for structural remodeling to occur. Loss or excess of RalGPS both abolish activity-induced synapse growth. Without altering levels of mature miR-219, stimulation elevates miR-219 loading in Argonaute (Ago1)-containing complexes that mediate miRNA gene silencing. We also find that elevated Protein Kinase A activity suppresses miR-219 association with Ago1 and blocks activity-induced synaptic growth, suggesting that miRNA loading and unloading in neurons are both controlled by activity-dependent regulation of Ago1.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: Mosaic divergent repeat interruptions of motif length and sequence, mDRILS, of XDP-linked repeats affect formation of DNA/RNA triplexes & quadruplexes.
abstract: An inserted SINE-VNTR-Alu(AGAGGG)n repeat into the TAF1 gene is the cause of X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism. Mosaic divergent repeat interruptions affecting both motif length and sequence (mDRILS) of the canonical repeat (AGAGGG)n arise and can diminish repeat instability and delay disease age of onset. The repeat itself may affect gain-of-function disease pathways. Consequently, XDP etiology may involve unusual structures formed by the repeats. To study the effects of mDRILS on the formation of unusual structures of the XDP TAF1-SVA repeat, we designed a series of G-rich DNA and RNA oligonucleotides having the pure canonical repeat 5'-(AGAGGG)4-3', or either of the most common mDRILS 5'-(AGAGGG)2AGGG(AGAGGG)-3'; and 5'-(AGAGGG)2AGG(AGAGGG)-3'. Circular dichroism, thermal melting, binding of the G-quadruplex ligand TMPyP4, shows the first canonical and AGGG-interrupted sequence assume K+-sensitive stable G-quadruplexes, whereas GA duplexes are the prominent structure in the AGG-interrupted form. The complementary C-rich strands, 5'-(CCCTCT)4-3', and 5'-(CCCTCT)2CCCT(CCCTCT)-3', and 5'-(CCCTCT)2CCT(CCCTCT)-3', assumed i-motif-compatible structure. Mixtures of the G- and C-rich complementary sequences, at 1:2 ratios, showed triplex-forming propensity for the canonical and AGGG-interrupted, but not the AGG-interrupted forms. The ability of mDRILS to elicit modifications of the disease-causing XDP TAF1-SVA repeat to enable or disable the formation of specific structures, such as quadruplex and triplex structures, may explain in part how mDRILS mediate their disease-modifying effects.

title: Soluble Epoxide Hydrolase Inhibition Accelerates Early Bone Repair in Critical-Size Calvarial Defects and Requires ENPP1 Activity for Osteoblast Mineralisation In Vitro.
abstract: Critical-size craniofacial bone defects heal poorly, and pharmacological strategies capable of accelerating bone repair remain limited. Soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) degrades epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), lipid mediators associated with inflammation resolution; however, the osteoblastic effectors that translate sEH inhibition into matrix mineralisation are unknown. We investigated whether pharmacological sEH inhibition accelerates craniofacial bone repair, and whether ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) a candidate regulator of pyrophosphate metabolism participates in this response. In vivo, bilateral 5-mm critical-size calvarial defects were created in male Wistar rats (n = 6 per group) treated with the sEH inhibitor TPPU (10 mg/kg/day, p.o.) or vehicle for 14 or 28 days. Repair was assessed by micro-computed tomography, histomorphometry, sEH immunohistochemistry and multiplex spatial RNA in situ hybridisation (RNAscope) of a predefined six-gene osteogenic panel (Spp1, Runx2, Col1a1, Alpl, Bglap, Enpp1). In vitro, human SAOS-2 osteoblastic cells were treated with TPPU and/or the ENPP1 inhibitor STF-1084 to assess viability, osteogenic gene expression, ENPP1 expression and enzymatic activity, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity and mineralised matrix formation. At 14 days, TPPU increased BV/TV, BS/TV and trabecular number and reduced trabecular separation and total porosity (p < 0.05); these differences were no longer detected at 28 days, whereas histomorphometry showed a greater newly formed bone area in TPPU-treated animals at both time points. sEH immunolabelling was reduced by TPPU at 14 and 28 days (p < 0.001), confirming target engagement. Spatially, Enpp1-positive cells were more abundant in TPPU-treated tissue at 14 days, the only panel gene reaching significance at the per-cell level. In vitro, TPPU increased ENPP1 mRNA and protein. STF-1084 dose-dependently reduced ENPP1 activity, ALP activity and mineralised matrix deposition without affecting viability, and co-treatment with TPPU did not restore mineralisation despite preserved or increased OSX, RUNX2 and BSP expression. Pharmacological sEH inhibition accelerates the early phase of craniofacial bone repair and is associated with increased ENPP1 expression in regenerating tissue. In human osteoblastic-SAOS cells, ENPP1 enzymatic activity is necessary for mineralisation and for the pro-mineralising effect of sEH inhibition, identifying ENPP1 as a candidate downstream effector of the sEH/EpFA axis and a target for further genetic validation.

title: Robust Prediction-Reliability Assessment in Biomedical Sensing and Classification Under Data Scarcity Using Conformal Prediction and Statistical Randomization.
abstract: Reliable assessment of prediction reliability is important in biomedical sensing and measurement applications, where machine learning models increasingly transform imaging, physiological, chemical, and molecular measurements into clinically relevant predictions. Such applications often operate under limited labeled data because sensor acquisition, experimental measurement, and expert annotation can be costly, while biological and measurement variability can further challenge model development. Under these conditions, reliability scores derived from standard inductive conformal prediction (ICP) can be sensitive to the particular division of available data into proper-training and calibration subsets. To address this issue, we propose three randomized ICP variants: bootstrapping ICP (BICP), randomized ICP (RICP), and out-of-bag ICP (OOB-ICP), to improve the informativeness and repeated-sampling stability of conformal-derived prediction-reliability scores under data scarcity. We benchmarked these methods using a controlled simulation and three real-world biomedical sensing and measurement applications: pneumonia diagnosis from X-ray radiography, alternative herbal medicine classification using a 16-channel semiconductor electronic-nose gas-sensing system, and breast cancer subtyping from RNA-seq molecular measurements. Results show that the proposed methods produce aggregate credibility scores that are informative of prediction correctness and less sensitive to randomness in training-data sampling. Empirical prediction-set coverage analyses further characterize the behavior of the aggregated conformity scores relative to nominal error levels without assuming that they retain the exact finite-sample validity of conventional conformal p-values. Among the evaluated methods, OOB-ICP achieved strong overall classification performance and informative, stable prediction-reliability scores, supporting statistical randomization as a practical strategy for stabilizing conformal-derived reliability assessment under limited training data in biomedical sensing and measurement applications.

title: An N-Terminal Acidic Patch Underlies Differential Inhibition of mRNA Nuclear Export by Human Coronavirus Nsp1 Proteins.
abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and related human coronaviruses (hCoVs) regulate host gene expression to facilitate viral replication and evade innate immunity. SARS-CoV-2 nonstructural protein 1 (Nsp1) suppresses host gene expression in part by inhibiting cellular mRNA nuclear export through targeting the mRNA export factor NXF1. However, whether this mechanism is conserved among Nsp1 proteins from diverse hCoVs remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that Nsp1 proteins from SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, and MERS-CoV, but not those from endemic hCoVs, induce pronounced nuclear accumulation of host poly(A) RNA without altering global transcript levels. Nsp1 proteins from these highly pathogenic hCoVs directly interact with NXF1, whereas endemic hCoV Nsp1 proteins show little or no detectable NXF1 interaction. Structural modeling and mutagenesis identify a conserved N-terminal acidic patch in Nsp1 that contacts the basic surface of the NXF1 RNA recognition motif. Disruption of this interface abolishes the Nsp1-NXF1 interaction and restores host mRNA export while preserving NXF1 interactions with core mRNA export factors. Together, our findings define a conserved structural mechanism by which highly pathogenic hCoV Nsp1 targets NXF1 to inhibit host mRNA export and provide a potential framework for broad-spectrum antiviral intervention.

title: Herpes Simplex Virus: Molecular Pathogenesis, Type-Specific Disease Burden, and Advances in Prevention and Treatment.
abstract: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a highly prevalent neurotropic DNA virus that causes orolabial herpes, genital herpes, keratitis, neonatal infection, meningitis and encephalitis. HSV-1 and HSV-2 share epithelial entry, lytic replication, immune evasion, lifelong sensory-ganglion latency and periodic reactivation, yet they differ in typical transmission routes, anatomical recurrence and public-health burden. Rather than mechanically separating both viruses throughout, this review emphasizes shared HSV biology and highlights type-specific differences where they affect clinical interpretation or intervention design. We connect glycoprotein-mediated entry, receptor use, axonal transport, immune evasion and latency with mucocutaneous, ocular, neurologic, neonatal and genital disease. We then synthesize lessons from failed glycoprotein-D vaccine trials, multivalent and mRNA platforms, helicase-primase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, RNA-based approaches, genome editing and latency-directed strategies. A mechanism-guided HSV strategy should reduce acquisition, shedding and recurrence, prevent ocular, neurologic and neonatal complications, manage antiviral resistance and ultimately address latent infection.

title: Virome Diversity and Host-Associated Heterogeneity in Mosquitoes and Biting Midges Across Yunnan, China.
abstract: Mosquitoes and biting midges harbor diverse viruses, but the factors shaping their viromes remain incompletely understood. We analyzed 35 pooled libraries from seven host groups across 15 locations in Yunnan, China, sampled in June 2025, using total-RNA sequencing, viral annotation, phylogenetics, and community analyses. We retained 1295 viral contigs grouped into 221 annotation-defined viral taxonomic units (VTUs) spanning 24 families; 107 VTUs were supported only by protein homology. Banna virus-related sequences, an Aedes-associated flavivirus, and four putative components of a divergent Jingmenvirus-related candidate were identified. Host group was associated with family-level virome composition after adjustment for location and sequencing depth (R2 = 0.213, p = 0.0052), and the association persisted across alternative feature definitions. Culex tritaeniorhynchus showed the greatest cumulative VTU richness, although its ranking changed when library number was equalized. Most VTUs detected in this host occurred at one sampled site, without a significant monotonic distance-decay pattern. This study expands knowledge of mosquito-associated and biting midge-associated viral diversity in Yunnan, identifies representative lineages for further characterization, and documents host-associated differences in the detected viromes.

title: Antiviral Sesquiterpene Lactones from Laurus nobilis L.: Inhibition of Hepatitis C Virus and Dengue Virus Replication.
abstract: Natural products remain indispensable scaffolds in antiviral drug discovery, particularly against high-burden viral pathogens. In this study, two major sesquiterpene lactones, dehydrocostus lactone (1) and costunolide (2), were isolated from Laurus nobilis L. leaves and evaluated for their antiviral potential against hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV). The structures of both compounds were confirmed by HRMS and 1D NMR spectroscopic analyses. In subgenomic replicon assays, the molecules inhibited HCV replication in the low-micromolar range (EC50=2.34 μM for 1 and 2.06 μM for 2) with favorable selectivity indices. In full-length HCV reporter systems, costunolide (2) displayed enhanced anti-HCV potency, reduced viral RNA and NS5A protein levels, and enhanced the suppressive effect of the clinically approved NS5A inhibitor, daclatasvir. Furthermore, costunolide (2) exhibited cross-flaviviridae activity, suppressing DENV replication (EC50=5.89 μM in replicon cells; EC50=1.27 μM post-infection in infectious virus assays), and demonstrated cooperative suppression of viral propagation along with reduced glutathione. Mechanistically, these results highlight the critical role of the sesquiterpene lactone core, and the observed enhanced combined activity between costunolide and reduced glutathione is consistent with a possible contribution of the NRF2/glutathione antioxidant axis to its anti-DENV action. Overall, this study highlights L. nobilis as a previously underexplored source of antiviral sesquiterpene lactones and establishes costunolide (2) as a promising lead against HCV and DENV, warranting further investigation across additional Flaviviridae members.

title: Molecular Characterization of Previous Unclassified Dicistroviruses in Water Reservoir in São Paulo, Brazil.
abstract: In this study, viral metagenomics was applied to identify viruses related to the Dicistroviridae family in freshwater samples collected from urban reservoirs of the state of São Paulo, Brazil. Through next-generation sequencing, five complete RNA genomes similar to Dicistroviridae were detected. These genomes range from 8.032 to 9.425 nucleotides in length, and each contains two open reading frames (ORFs) with conserved protein domains and internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) characteristic of Dicistroviridae. Phylogenetic and genetic identity analyses based on the amino acid sequences of the nonstructural (ORF1) and structural (ORF2) polyproteins suggest that these five genomes represent four putative novel species provisionally named Hydro virus 1 to Hydro virus 4. These findings enhance our understanding of the diversity and distribution of Dicistroviridae in aquatic environments.

title: Niosomal Mexiletine Attenuates Rotenone-Induced Parkinsonism via Modulation of the circDLGAP4/miR-134-5p/p-CREB Axis and Restoration of Mitochondrial-Autophagic Homeostasis.
abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease (PD) is distinguished by progressive dopaminergic degeneration driven by the convergence of oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired autophagy. Mexiletine (Mexil), which has demonstrated antioxidant properties, has not been systematically investigated yet for its potential to mitigate mitochondrial-dysfunction-related neurodegeneration in PD. Using an integrated computational and experimental approach, we characterized, for the first time, the neuroprotective mechanisms of Mexil's action against rotenone (Rot)-induced Parkinsonism and employed niosomes as a nanocarrier platform to enhance mexil delivery and augment its neuroprotective potential in a Parkinson's disease model. Methods: Molecular docking identified candidate molecular targets underlying niosomal Mexil's neuroprotective potential. Sprague-Dawley male rats were assigned to control, Rot, and Rot plus niosomal Mexil (30 and 50 mg/kg) groups. Motor performance was evaluated, while dopaminergic degeneration, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy were assessed biochemically, histopathologically, and immunohistochemically. Results: Docking revealed promising interactions between Mexil and both phosphorylated cAMP response element-binding protein (p-CREB) and alpha-synuclein, with binding scores of -5.2 and -4.9 kcal/mol, respectively. Niosomal Mexil improved motor function, restored dopamine and tyrosine hydroxylase levels, and curtailed alpha-synuclein accumulation. Most notably, niosomal Mexil engaged a previously unexplored circular RNA DLGAP4/microRNA-134-5p/p-CREB axis, promoted mitochondrial biogenesis via the phosphorylated AMP-activated protein kinase (p-AMPK)/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α)/sirtuin-1 (SIRT-1) pathway, and rebalanced mitochondrial dynamics. These changes were accompanied by restored autophagic axis and suppressed oxidative stress and inflammation. Conclusions: Niosomal Mexil confers neuroprotection against Rot-induced Parkinsonism by orchestrating oxidative, mitochondrial, autophagic, and inflammatory pathways, positioning it as a mechanistically novel disease-modifying candidate warranting further preclinical evaluation in PD.

title: RNA Splicing of the MsndhB Gene and Photosynthetic Characteristics in Alfalfa (Medicago sativa) Under High- and Low-Temperature Stress.
abstract: RNA splicing of chloroplast-encoded genes contributes to plant responses to abiotic stress, yet its regulation remains poorly understood in forage legumes. Here, we investigated RNA splicing of the chloroplast ndhB gene in alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) under abiotic stress and its association with photosynthetic and physiological responses under temperature stress. Using cultivar 'Xinjiang Daye', we characterized MsndhB structure and analyzed splicing efficiency across tissues, developmental stages, and four stress treatments (high temperature, low temperature, salt, and drought). Under high- and low-temperature stress, photosynthetic gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, ATP, and malondialdehyde (MDA) were measured to evaluate associations with MsndhB splicing efficiency. The results showed that high temperature reduced splicing efficiency and caused pre-mRNA accumulation, whereas low temperature enhanced splicing; salt and drought affected transcript abundance but not splicing efficiency. Splicing efficiency was higher in green tissues and at the branching stage. Under temperature stress, splicing efficiency was correlated with photosynthetic and oxidative stress indicators, but these associations do not provide evidence of functional control. These findings suggest that MsndhB splicing is temperature-responsive and may be involved in chloroplast responses to temperature stress, providing a foundation for elucidating the role of post-transcriptional regulation of chloroplast genes in alfalfa responses to temperature stress.

title: A Novel Rubodvirus Associated with Progressive Leaf Whitening Disease in Bougainvillea: Genomic Insights and Phylogenetic Relationships.
abstract: Bougainvillea sp. is an important ornamental and landscape plant in tropical and subtropical regions. In October 2024, progressive leaf whitening resembling viral infection was observed in Haikou, Hainan Province, China. To investigate the factors associated with progressive leaf whitening in bougainvillea (particularly viral pathogens), we performed virome analysis of two symptomatic leaf samples using total RNA sequencing with ribosomal RNA depletion on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. A novel tripartite negative-sense RNA virus was identified and tentatively named Bougainvillea progressive whitening virus (BgPWV), belonging to the genus Rubodvirus in the family Phenuiviridae. Its genome comprises RNA1-RNA3, each containing a single open reading frame flanked by untranslated regions, encoding the large protein (302 kDa), movement protein (43 kDa), and nucleocapsid protein (32 kDa), respectively. The 5' and 3' terminal sequences of each genomic RNA are highly conserved and complementary. Molecular screening of 54 bougainvillea plants showed that all 14 symptomatic plants tested positive for BgPWV, whereas all 40 asymptomatic samples tested were negative; three symptomatic plants were co-infected with Bougainvillea chlorotic vein banding virus. These results indicate a significant association between BgPWV and leaf whitening and expand the known host range and genetic diversity of rubodviruses, providing a foundation for future studies on bougainvillea viral diseases.

title: Integrative Multi-Database Bioinformatics Characterization of FANCE in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Prognostic, Epigenetic, Immune, and ncRNA Associations.
abstract: Background and Objectives: The Fanconi anemia complementation group E (FANCE) is a protein component of the Fanconi anemia (FA) DNA repair complex and contributes to genome integrity. However, its molecular and clinical relevance in liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) remains incompletely understood. This study characterized the FANCE expression, prognosis, epigenetics, immune responses, noncoding RNA (ncRNA) networks, and other related molecular processes in LIHC. Materials and Methods: An integrative multi-database bioinformatics analysis was conducted using public databases and web-based platforms. FANCE expression, DNA methylation, co-expression profiles, and functional enrichment; immune cell infiltration; miRNA-ncRNA, chemical-gene, and protein-protein interactions; treatment response; and survival were evaluated. Results: FANCE expression was higher in LIHC than in non-tumor liver tissues, and this was linked to shorter survival duration. Promoter methylation was lower in LIHC, and select CpG sites were related to FANCE expression and survival. Immune analyses identified heterogeneous relationships between FANCE and inferred immune cell populations. hsa-miR-101-3p was reduced in LIHC, negatively correlated with FANCE, and linked to prolonged survival; subsequent network analysis identified candidate lncRNAs, small ncRNAs, circRNA-linked genes, and pseudogenes. FANCE-related transcriptional profiles were enriched in the cell cycle, DNA replication, FA, and other DNA-repair processes, whereas negatively correlated genes were mainly linked to hepatic metabolic functions. Exploratory treatments identified drug-dependent survival patterns related to FANCE expression and elevated levels in responders to specific immune-checkpoint inhibitors, although the discriminatory performance was modest. Conclusions: Increased FANCE expression in LIHC was linked to molecular features involving DNA methylation, immune cell composition, ncRNA-related interactions, and DNA repair programs as well as shorter survival. These findings provide an integrated molecular context for FANCE in LIHC but do not establish a causal regulation or therapeutic predictive value. Independent clinical and experimental validation studies are warranted to determine its biological and clinical significance.

title: Beyond Homologous Recombination: Functional Modules of Olaparib Resistance Revealed by CRISPR Screens.
abstract: Clinical use of PARP inhibitors (PARPi), including olaparib, has improved outcomes for patients with BRCA1/2-mutant and homologous recombination (HR)-deficient tumors. However, acquired resistance remains a major limitation to their efficacy. CRISPR-Cas9 screening approaches have been developed to identify genetic drivers of PARPi resistance. However, differences in experimental conditions, library coverage, and selection design complicate comparisons across studies. In this review, we present a harmonized reanalysis of CRISPR knockout olaparib resistance screens to identify recurrent resistance-associated genes and pathways. Datasets with raw data were collected from the BioGRID ORCS database. Resistance hits identified in at least two screens were subjected to Reactome pathway-enrichment analysis and organized into functional modules. Using this approach, we identified eight modules: DNA-damage repair and replication stress; cell-cycle regulation; chromatin remodeling and histone modification; post-translational regulation; mitochondrial function; TGF-β and mTOR signaling; RNA processing and nucleocytoplasmic transport; and emerging adaptive mechanisms. Importantly, mitochondrial function genes were observed as recurrent hits, but their relation to olaparib resistance is underinvestigated. Our integrative analysis suggests that PARPi resistance is a complex, adaptive phenotype shaped by recurrent but context-dependent vulnerabilities across multiple cellular programs. This framework prioritizes candidate resistance drivers for validation and highlights directions for the design of combination therapies aimed at overcoming PARPi resistance.

title: Non-Canonical HIF2 Accumulation in Breast Cancer Cells.
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming drives cancer aggressiveness. While hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF1) is commonly associated with glycolysis regulation, the under-investigated HIF2 isoform may also modulate the metabolic profile of breast cancer. We investigated the role of non-canonical HIF2 activation in metabolic adaptation to nutrient availability by culturing MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells under normoxia with varying glucose and glutamine concentrations. Using RNA interference, we downregulated HIF2 and analyzed HIF isoforms and metabolic targets (GLUT1, HK2, PKM2, PDK1) at the transcriptional and protein levels. We observed a new, non-canonical accumulation of HIF2 in MDA-MB-231 cells associated with glucose and glutamine restriction, a phenomenon absent in MCF-7 cells. In MDA-MB-231 cells, silencing HIF2A under standard conditions significantly decreased PDK1 mRNA expression. At the protein level, HIF2 downregulation altered metabolic targets in a context-dependent manner under nutrient restriction. Adding a hypoxia-mimetic (CoCl2) did not fully restore the protein expression patterns, suggesting that HIF2 accumulation may contribute to these context-dependent shifts. HIF2 downregulation decreased glycolytic efficiency under low-glucose conditions. Our findings suggest that HIF2 might modulate the metabolic plasticity of MDA-MB-231 cells through distinct changes in gene expression and post-translational mechanisms. This provides support for investigating the HIF2 isoform while studying breast cancer metabolism and considering it as a potential target for treating triple-negative breast cancer.

title: Breed-by-Altitude Interaction Reveals Cardiac miRNA-mRNA Regulatory Hubs Associated with Hypoxia Adaptation in Tibetan Pigs.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are important post-transcriptional regulators of cardiac responses to hypoxia, but how breed and altitude interact to shape cardiac miRNA expression remains unclear. We used a 2 × 2 factorial design involving Tibetan and Yorkshire pigs raised at high (3000 m) or low (100 m) altitude. Small RNA sequencing identified 1104 miRNAs, including 370 known and 734 putative novel miRNA candidates. Pairwise comparisons revealed greater breed-related divergence at high altitude and a stronger altitude-associated miRNA response in Tibetan pigs than in Yorkshire pigs. The breed-by-altitude interaction analysis identified 94 breed-by-altitude interaction-responsive miRNAs, including 25 not detected by pairwise comparisons. K-means clustering further identified a Tibetan high-altitude-enriched miRNA module whose predicted targets were associated with hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), adrenergic, calcium, and metabolic pathways. Integration with previously published cardiac messenger RNA (mRNA) differential-expression results for high-altitude Tibetan versus Yorkshire pigs, generated from the corresponding biological samples, prioritized 319 anti-correlated miRNA-mRNA pairs involving 19 miRNAs and 224 mRNAs, with ssc-miR-671-5p as the leading network hub. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), correlation analysis, and miRanda prediction prioritized three candidate regulatory pairs: ssc-miR-671-5p-ATP1B2, novel-miR-212-ADCY6, and ssc-miR-296-3p-PFKM. These findings characterize breed-dependent, altitude-associated cardiac miRNA expression patterns and prioritize candidate miRNA-mRNA relationships for future functional investigation.

title: Nanopore Sequencing for Epigenetic Decoding: Applications, Analytical Constraints, and Translational Prospects.
abstract: Epigenetic regulation involves multiple molecular layers, including DNA and RNA modifications, histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), and chromatin accessibility. These processes contribute to cell identity, development, and disease, but their measurement remains technically challenging because sequence context, molecular modification, chromatin state, and transcript structure are often assayed separately. As a representative third-generation sequencing technology, nanopore sequencing is profoundly reshaping the interpretation of the epigenetic code through its distinctive capabilities, including long-read sequencing, direct single-molecule signal detection, and the identification of nucleic acid modifications without bisulfite conversion or PCR in appropriate workflows. This review summarizes applications of nanopore sequencing in epigenomics and epitranscriptomics and evaluates emerging nanopore-based approaches for protein and histone sensing. We focus on what can currently be measured, the experimental and computational requirements for reliable decoding, and the limitations that must be addressed before broader multi-omic and clinical use.

title: Recent Advances in Lipid Nanoparticles for Cancer Vaccines: From Antigen Delivery to Personalized Immunotherapy.
abstract: In recent years, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have shown great promise as highly flexible delivery systems for cancer vaccines, which enable effective cargo delivery and allow for controlling their distribution, cell-targeting ability and immunogenicity. Innovations in ionizable lipid chemistry, biodegradable formulations, RNA engineering and LNP design resulted in improvements in RNA encapsulation, endosomal escape, delivery outside the liver, and targeting of lymphoid organs and antigen-presenting cells. All these achievements led to an expansion of strategies for developing cancer vaccines from using only mRNA to personal neoantigen vaccines, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), peptide/protein vaccines, and multi-purpose platforms that combine antigen delivery and modulation of the immune system. LNPs are also studied as tools for altering the tumor microenvironment (TME) and boosting anti-tumor immunity through local delivery of cytokines and innate immune modulators. Preliminary clinical results with personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines show strong potential for this approach. However, inflammatory toxicity, suitability for repeated dosing, off-target delivery, difficulties with large-scale production, formulation stability, personalized production schedule and regulatory issues are still significant challenges. New biodegradable and PEG-free formulations, innovations in manufacturing and lyophilization technology, and AI-based approaches in lipid screening could help overcome some of these problems.

title: Profiling Amino Acid Substitutions in Proteomic Datasets of Alzheimer's Disease Reveals Biological Significance.
abstract: Background: Amino acid (AA) substitutions in Alzheimer's disease (AD) have been studied almost exclusively at the DNA and RNA levels, and the proteome-level substitution landscape remains largely uncharacterized. Methods: We applied an open-search substitutomics pipeline (PIPI-C with Comet re-scoring, 1% PSM-level FDR) to two independent AD brain proteomic datasets, the AMP-AD superior temporal gyrus cohort (244 individuals) and PXD013753, excluding substitutions whose mass shifts coincide with common post-translational modifications. Results: We quantified 789 substitution-bearing peptidoforms from 185 proteins, corresponding to 784 protein-level substitution events. N > M was the most frequent N > X substitution in both datasets. In an institution-stratified case-control meta-analysis, 138 peptidoforms were more and 142 less abundant in AD than in neuropathological controls. Of 774 genome-mappable events, 710 (91.7%) were recorded in neither UniProt nor gnomAD, and only five matched a population variant with allele frequency ≥ 0.1%. The unrestricted search recovered six literature-reported sites in GFAP, ACTG1, and HBB. Conclusions: Proteome-level profiling reveals substitution events in AD brains that catalogued germline variation does not explain; their molecular origin requires orthogonal validation.

title: Curcumin Alleviates Ochratoxin A-Induced Oxidative Injury in Porcine Kidney Epithelial Cells in Association with Restored Nrf2/NQO1/HO-1-Related Antioxidant Expression.
abstract: Ochratoxin A (OTA) damages renal epithelial cells and disrupts redox homeostasis. We examined whether curcumin (Cur) reduces OTA-induced injury in porcine kidney epithelial PK-15 cells and whether protection accompanies changes in antioxidant expression. Preliminary concentration screening gave an OTA half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 10.83 μg/mL. Cells received OTA (8 μg/mL), Cur (10 μmol/L), their combination, or control treatment. Cell viability, apoptosis, oxidant burden, mitochondrial membrane potential, and biochemical markers were assessed alongside quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) and Western blotting. A previously published RNA-sequencing dataset was reanalyzed to examine redox-related responses. OTA reduced viability and mitochondrial membrane potential, increased apoptosis, and impaired antioxidant defenses. Cur attenuated these changes, lowered oxidant-associated fluorescence, malondialdehyde, and lactate dehydrogenase release, and improved glutathione status. The shared RNA-sequencing dataset contained 11,707 differentially expressed genes in OTA versus control and 498 in OTA+Cur versus OTA, with 380 genes common to both comparisons. Targeted assays showed higher Nrf2, NQO1, and HO-1 mRNA and total-protein abundance with Cur than with OTA alone. These results associate Cur-mediated protection with recovery of antioxidant expression in PK-15 cells. They do not establish Nrf2 activation or a causal requirement for this pathway.

title: Formononetin Protects Osteoblasts Against Oxidative Stress and Attenuates Ovariectomy-Induced Bone Loss in Association with MAPK/AP-1 and NRF2 Signaling.
abstract: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMOP) is associated with estrogen deficiency and oxidative stress (OS), which impair osteoblast survival and osteogenic function. Formononetin (FMN) is a phytoestrogen with antioxidant properties, but its protective effects on osteoblasts under OS and the signaling pathways associated with these effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we evaluated the effects of FMN in ovariectomized (OVX) mice and in a tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BOOH)-induced oxidative injury model in MC3T3-E1 cells. Bone microarchitecture, histology, serum OS markers, cell viability, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, apoptosis, mitochondrial morphology, and osteogenic differentiation were assessed. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and pharmacological pathway-modulation experiments were used to investigate signaling changes associated with FMN treatment. FMN attenuated trabecular bone deterioration and systemic oxidative imbalance in OVX mice. In MC3T3-E1 cells, FMN improved cell viability, reduced ROS accumulation and apoptosis, alleviated mitochondrial damage, and preserved osteogenic differentiation following t-BOOH exposure. FMN treatment was accompanied by reduced phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2), p38, and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), together with reduced expression of activator protein 1 (AP-1)-related proteins, including c-Fos, c-Jun, and phosphorylated c-Jun. Pharmacological reactivation of p38/JNK signaling with anisomycin attenuated several antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and pro-osteogenic effects associated with FMN treatment, whereas nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) inhibition partially diminished FMN-mediated protection. Collectively, these findings support an association between the protective effects of FMN and modulation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/AP-1 and NRF2-associated signaling.

title: Methylglyoxal as a Potential Mediator of Metabolic Memory in Diabetes-Related Complications: From Oxidative Stress to Macromolecular Glycation and Epigenetic Remodeling.
abstract: Diabetes-related complications often continue to progress despite improved glycemic control, a phenomenon known as metabolic memory. Increasing evidence suggests that methylglyoxal (MGO), a highly reactive dicarbonyl generated during glycolysis, may be an important mediator of this process. Hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress promotes MGO formation, where MGO further promotes mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species production, establishing a self-reinforcing cycle of stress. In addition, MGO modifies proteins, impairing their structure and function and promoting persistent inflammatory signaling through advanced glycation end-products. More recently, nucleic acids have emerged as important targets of dicarbonyl stress, with MGO-induced DNA and RNA glycation contributing to genomic instability and altered cellular function. Furthermore, MGO-mediated histone glycation and epigenetic remodeling may provide a mechanistic link between hyperglycemia and long-lasting changes in gene expression. These mechanisms are particularly relevant in diabetic kidney disease, where MGO contributes to inflammation, fibrosis and renal injury. However, direct evidence that MGO-induced molecular alterations and their functional consequences persist after normalization of both glucose and MGO remains limited. This review discusses the role of MGO in metabolic memory, focusing on oxidative stress, protein glycation, nucleic acid damage and epigenetic remodeling, and highlights emerging therapeutic strategies targeting dicarbonyl stress to prevent the progression of diabetes-related complications.

title: Single-Nuclei RNA Sequencing Data Analysis: Cardiomyocyte-Specific Modified-mNA Targeting Cyclin D2 Turns Subpopulations of Adult Pig Cardiomyocytes, Fibroblasts, and Smooth Muscle Cells Back to Neonatal Characteristics at Day 2 After SMRT Intervention.
abstract: Naturally, pig hearts cannot recover from ischemic reperfusion injury; however, pig hearts receiving cardiomyocyte-specific modified-RNA (CM-SMRTs) targeting Cyclin D2 (CCND2CM-SMRTs) demonstrated significantly better cardiac function, compared to the untreated hearts receiving Green Fluorescent Protein-induced modified RNA (GFPCM-SMRTs). In this report, we generated and analyzed single-nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) data to examine the mechanism by which CCND2CM-SMRTs regulate the cardiomyocyte cell cycle and improve cardiac function in the whole heart. The snRNAseq data from CCND2CM-SMRTs-treated pig hearts (~2-month-old) were integrated with the data from age-matched GFPCM-SMRTs-treated hearts, harvested on day 2 and day 28 after treatment, as well as with naïve neonatal day 1 and 2 (with regenerative potential) and with naïve 2-month-old (without regenerative potential) data. SnRNAseq data from all cardiac cell types were analyzed using an Autoencoder pipeline. Six cardiomyocytes (CM1-CM6), four fibroblasts (FB1-FB4), six smooth muscle cells (SMC1-SMC4), five endothelial cells (EC1-EC5), four macrophages (Mph1-Mph4), and two T-cell (Tcell1 and Tcell2) clusters were defined. While CCND2 is well-known as a major cell cycle driver from G1 to S phase, the snRNAseq data did not indicate any significant changes regarding cell cycle activity among CCND2CM-SMRTs-treated pigs, compared to GFPCM-SMRTs pigs, on day 2. Rather, clusters CM1, FB1, and SMC1 were observed in neonatal pig hearts and at the injury-border zone, where CM-SMRTs were delivered, in CCND2CM-SMRT-treated hearts on day 2 after treatment; these clusters did not appear in any remote zones, which were not subjected to ischemic reperfusion and CM-SMRTs effect, or in any untreated and naïve hearts. However, on day 28, clusters of FB1, and SMC1 were no longer observed, and only CM1 were prominently seen in border zone of CCND2CM-SMRT-treated hearts. Intercellular communication analysis revealed that CM1 may impact other non-cardiomyocyte clusters early after SMRT intervention via the BMP and PDGF signaling pathways. Thus, the analysis suggested that CCND2CM-SMRTs may drive a subset of pig cardiac cells toward a neonatal state, in which pig hearts still retain regenerative capacity.

title: Immune-Inflammatory, Autophagy, and JNK Remodeling in Ischemic and Nonischemic Human Myocardium.
abstract: This study investigated ischemic versus nonischemic human myocardium across disease phenotypes, sex, and race, prioritizing genes involved in immune-inflammatory signaling, autophagy, JNK-associated stress responses, innate immune recognition, and solute transport. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed in 75 human heart tissue samples, including 13 controls, 18 ischemic samples, and 44 nonischemic samples. Primary models tested ischemic versus control, nonischemic versus control, and nonischemic versus ischemic contrasts. Secondary models evaluated sex- and race-associated expression while adjusting for disease status and sequencing batch. Ischemic versus control comparison identified 3974 genes and nonischemic versus control identified 4276 genes at adjusted p < 0.05, while nonischemic versus ischemic identified only two genes. After adjustment for disease status and sequencing batch, 108 genes (including 64 autosomal genes) were associated with sex and 128 with race at FDR < 0.05. In the adjusted race analysis, SLC39A4 was higher and MAP1LC3B2 lower in White samples after FDR correction. Ischemic and nonischemic myocardium showed extensive shared remodeling with exploratory nominal differences. Sex and race were associated with additional variation in immune, proteostatic, and nutrient-transport programs. BAG3 transcript abundance was not significantly altered, consistent with prior evidence that transcript and protein abundance may be uncoupled in failing myocardium.

title: SpliceCOV: Supervised Filtering of RNA-Seq-Derived Transcript Features Improves Transcriptome Assembly.
abstract: Background/Objectives: High-throughput RNA sequencing enables transcript discovery and quantification, but the resulting coverage profiles often contain substantial transcriptional noise, making it difficult to distinguish genuine transcript features from spurious signals. These noisy signals can propagate into transcriptome assemblies, increasing the number of false transcript models and reducing annotation precision. Methods: We present SpliceCOV, a supervised framework for filtering RNA-Seq-derived transcript features. Rather than performing general-purpose segmentation of RNA-Seq coverage, SpliceCOV uses coverage- and junction-derived features to distinguish likely genuine splice sites and transcript boundaries from noisy candidates. We benchmarked SpliceCOV against established changepoint methods and evaluated whether SpliceCOV-filtered features improve downstream transcriptome assembly with StringTie. Results: Across human GTEx tissue datasets, SpliceCOV substantially reduced likely false-positive splice sites while retaining most annotated sites. We included segmentation-based methods as baselines to assess whether generic coverage changepoints can support RNA-Seq transcript-feature filtering. Because these methods are unsupervised whereas SpliceCOV is trained using annotation-derived labels, the comparisons are intended to assess suitability for this specific filtering task rather than to provide a general ranking of the underlying algorithms. Under this evaluation framework, SpliceCOV retained more annotation-supported splice sites at comparable levels of filtering. For transcript start and end sites, SpliceCOV reduced the majority of false positives while retaining substantial overlap with reference annotations. When SpliceCOV-filtered splice sites and transcript boundaries were supplied to StringTie, transcript-level precision increased across the evaluated tissues while the number of reference-matching transcripts remained broadly similar. The model also showed transferability across tissues and chromosomes, and could be applied to mouse RNA-Seq without retraining, although downstream assembly performance was lower than in human datasets. Conclusions: SpliceCOV provides a supervised approach for filtering noisy RNA-Seq-derived transcript features before transcriptome assembly. By improving the quality of splice-site and transcript-boundary evidence supplied to downstream assembly, SpliceCOV can increase transcript-level precision while preserving transcript recovery.

title: Complete Mitochondrial Genome of a French Bulldog with Carcinoma planoepitheliale keratodes G1: A Descriptive Case Report.
abstract: French Bulldogs, like other brachycephalic breeds, are predisposed to a variety of genetic and tumour-related disorders. While mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations have been documented in canine tumours, no prior study has examined the entire mitochondrial genome in this breed. In this study, we analysed mtDNA obtained from blood and tumour tissue of a 10-year-old male French Bulldog diagnosed with carcinoma planoepitheliale keratodes (G1). Complete sequencing and comparative bioinformatic analysis revealed 22 sequence variants, including nine in protein-coding genes, two in RNA-coding genes, two in the control region, and nine within the variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) region. Identical variants were present in both blood and tumour tissue, indicating that no detectable tumour-specific mtDNA mutations were observed. Notably, the m.1397A>T transversion in the 16S rRNA gene and an insertion (m.2679_2680insG) in the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene were identified, both mapping to conserved loci in the human mitochondrial genome. Among the coding variants, four nonsynonymous variants (including p.Cys55Tyr and p.Ser471Asn) were detected, two of which affected highly conserved amino acid positions. Most nonsynonymous changes were localised in random coil regions and internal mitochondrial compartments, whereas synonymous changes appeared mainly within transmembrane helices. The control region displayed the highest degree of polymorphism, including eight positions with A/G heteroplasmy and one length variant due to polyT extension. These findings represent the first documentation of full mitochondrial genome sequence variants in a French Bulldog with cancer providing descriptive data for future breed population and oncological research. Further studies are warranted to determine whether these alterations are breed- or tumour-specific.

title: Association of Copy Number Variations in PTEN with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with a strong genetic basis. While copy number variations (CNVs) significantly contribute to ASD risk, the specific role of individual genes within these variants remains unclear. This study investigates the contribution of CNVs in the PTEN gene to ASD pathophysiology by integrating population-level genetic analysis with multi-dimensional biological evidence. Methods: The biological plausibility of PTEN in ASD was first assessed using public multi-omics data, including tissue expression profiles, protein-protein interaction networks, and published cell-type-specific differential-expression data derived from single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Subsequently, a group-matched case-control study was conducted in a Han Chinese population (121 ASD cases and 110 controls) to evaluate the association between PTEN CNVs and ASD susceptibility. One-way ANOVA was performed to compare the differences in ASD clinical phenotype scores among groups with different CNV types of PTEN. Results: Integrative biological analyses revealed that PTEN is enriched in ASD-relevant brain regions (e.g., cerebellum) and exhibits cell-type-specific expression in neurons and glia. Furthermore, protein network analysis confirmed its central position within the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, a critical regulator of neurodevelopment. In the Han Chinese population, no significant association was detected between PTEN CNVs and ASD risks or clinical phenotype scores. Conclusions:PTEN CNVs may not be independently associated with ASD, but may contribute to susceptibility through broader neurodevelopmental networks and molecular pathways.

title: Stereoselective C2'-Alkylation of Nucleosides Enabled by Electrochemical Ni-Catalyzed C(sp3)-C(sp3) Cross-Coupling.
abstract: Chemical modification at the C2' position of nucleosides is critical to nucleic acid therapeutic development, yet general and stereoselective methods for C2'-alkylation remain limited due to synthetic challenges associated with nucleoside substrates. Herein, we report an electrochemical Ni-catalyzed stereoselective C(sp3)-C(sp3) cross-coupling strategy for efficient C2'-α-alkylation of nucleosides. Readily accessible C2'-bromonucleosides and NHPI esters derived from abundant carboxylic acids serve as coupling partners under mild electrochemical conditions, enabling modular installation of diverse alkyl groups with broad functional-group tolerance and excellent diastereoselectivity. The protocol accommodates multiple nucleobases, is scalable, and provides products directly compatible with oligonucleotide synthesis. Biophysical studies indicate that these modifications can modulate DNA/RNA duplex thermal stability and improve resistance to exonuclease degradation. This electrochemical cross-coupling strategy provides an approach to C2'-alkyl-modified nucleosides and expands the toolbox for functional nucleic acid design.

title: Converging lines of evidence fail to detect nanovirus replication in its insect vector.
abstract: Nanoviruses have a multipartite circular ssDNA genome and are transmitted by aphids in a circulative manner. Although generally considered non-propagative within their vectors, direct experimental evidence supporting the absence of viral replication remains limited. This question is particularly relevant for multipartite viruses because replication within vectors could theoretically help maintain genome integrity during transmission, decreasing dilution effects and the probability of genome segment loss. Here, we investigated whether faba bean necrotic stunt virus (FBNSV, genus Nanovirus, family Nanoviridae) replicates in aphids using several independent approaches. Viral load dynamics were quantitative PCR-monitored after virus acquisition, the replication-associated protein M-Rep was searched for within gut and salivary gland cells by immunofluorescence, viral DNA localization and strand specificity were analysed using HCR-DNA-FISH (hybridization chain reaction fluorescence in situ hybridization) and confocal microscopy, viral transcription was investigated by Illumina mRNA sequencing, and viral DNA replication was analysed by Nanopore sequencing. All approaches converged towards the same conclusion. Viral loads did not increase after acquisition, M-Rep was undetectable in aphid tissues, viral DNA accumulated outside nuclei, no negative-strand viral DNA was detected, and only negligible quantities of viral transcripts and dsDNA molecules were detected in RNA-seq and Nanopore-seq datasets from viruliferous aphids, although these molecules were readily detected in FBNSV-infected plants used as the acquisition source. While none of these approaches could alone suffice to definitely exclude a weak, localized and/or transient replication, they together strongly support the conclusion that FBNSV is transmitted in a genuinely circulative non-propagative manner.

title: The 3' UTR Pseudoknot-Containing Region of Arteriviruses Acts as a PAMP to Activate RIG-I- and TLR8-Dependent Type I Interferon Responses.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) and other members of the Arteriviridae family cause substantial economic losses in livestock. However, their pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated whether the 3' untranslated region (UTR) pseudoknot structures of Arteriviruses act as PAMPs and explored the underlying innate immune recognition mechanisms. Bioinformatics predictions (RNAalifold, RNArtist, and RNAComposer) revealed that the 3' UTR pseudoknot structures are conserved across all four Arteriviruses. In vitro transcribed pseudoknot RNAs significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of type I interferons (IFNα/β) and interferon-stimulated genes (protein kinase R, PKR; interferon-stimulated gene 15, ISG15; interferon-stimulated gene 56, ISG56) in Marc145 cells. Screening of RNA-sensing pattern recognition receptors (retinoic acid-inducible gene I, RIG-I; melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5, MDA5; Toll-like receptor 3/7/8/9, TLR3/7/8/9) in pseudoknot RNA-stimulated cells showed that RIG-I and TLR8 were significantly upregulated, whereas MDA5, TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9 were not. Short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated knockdown of RIG-I or TLR8 significantly reduced pseudoknot-induced expression of IFNβ, PKR, and ISG56, confirming that both receptors are functionally required for this response. Upregulation of myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88), interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7), and signal transducer and activator of transcription 2 (STAT2) suggested that IFNα/β and downstream interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) were induced via the TLR8-MyD88-IRF7 and RIG-I-IRF7 signaling pathways. Moreover, small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analysis of the PRRSV pseudoknot RNA complexed with the porcine RIG-I regulatory domain was consistent with the formation of a complex between the pseudoknot RNA and RIG-I. In conclusion, this study identified the 3' UTR pseudoknot-containing region of Arteriviruses as a conserved PAMP that activates RIG-I- and TLR8-dependent type I IFN responses, providing a mechanistic basis and potential targets for antiviral therapy and vaccine adjuvant development against Arterivirus infections.

title: SOCS3 Suppression Is Associated with Hippocampal Inflammation in a Mouse Model of Intermittent Hypoxia.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Intermittent hypoxia (IH), a feature of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), is associated with hippocampal inflammation and cognitive dysfunction. We examined SOCS3 expression and a possible MALAT1/EZH2/H3K27me3 regulatory relationship in a mouse IH model and BV2 cells. Methods: C57BL/6J mice were exposed to IH for 4 weeks, followed by Morris water maze testing and analysis of hippocampal tissue. BV2 cells were exposed to IH and used for transfection, RNA immunoprecipitation, and chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments. Results: In mice, IH was associated with poorer water maze performance, lower hippocampal SOCS3, and higher levels of inflammatory markers, MALAT1, and H3K27me3. Similar molecular changes were observed in BV2 cells. SOCS3 overexpression reduced TRAF6, total NF-κB p65, TNF-α, and IL-1β protein levels in BV2 cells. MALAT1 was enriched by EZH2 immunoprecipitation, H3K27me3 was enriched at the SOCS3 promoter, and MALAT1 knockdown reduced total H3K27me3 while increasing SOCS3 protein. Conclusions: These findings associate reduced SOCS3 with hippocampal inflammation after IH and support further investigation of MALAT1 and EZH2 in its regulation. The cellular source of the in vivo inflammatory markers and the causal role of EZH2 require direct testing.

title: DONSON-Associated MISSLA with Co-Occurring p.Arg442Ter and p.Lys489Thr Variants: Longitudinal Clinical and Genomic Characterization.
abstract: Background: Microcephaly, short stature, and limb abnormalities syndrome (MISSLA) is an ultra-rare developmental disorder associated with biallelic DONSON variation and characterized by prenatal-onset growth restriction, congenital microcephaly, variable skeletal abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental impairment. We describe the longitudinal clinical and genomic features of an Ecuadorian child with a phenotype highly compatible with DONSON-associated MISSLA. Methods: This retrospective longitudinal case report included clinical information from the prenatal period through February 2026. Serial anthropometric, neurodevelopmental, nutritional, skeletal, and neuroimaging findings were reviewed. Clinical whole-exome sequencing with mitochondrial DNA analysis was performed during infancy. DONSON variants were evaluated using current transcript nomenclature, population and clinical databases, and published variant-specific evidence. Because patient-derived RNA was unavailable, the predicted susceptibility of NM_017613.4:c.1324C>T (p.Arg442Ter) to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) was assessed using NMDetective-B. Results: The proband had severe prenatal growth restriction and congenital microcephaly, followed by persistent profound short stature, marked postnatal weight impairment, feeding difficulties, developmental delay with continued acquisition of motor and language abilities, and relatively mild skeletal involvement. At 7 years and 4 months, weight was 10.3 kg (Z = -8.02) and height was 91.5 cm (Z = -5.00). Whole-exome sequencing identified heterozygous DONSON c.1324C>T (p.Arg442Ter) and c.1466A>C (p.Lys489Thr), together with c.82A>C (p.Ser28Arg). The recurrent intronic c.786-33A>G variant was not detected, although limited coverage precluded definitive exclusion. Parental segregation data were unavailable, and compound heterozygosity was therefore not established. NMDetective-B yielded a score of 0.65, predicting that p.Arg442Ter is susceptible to NMD. Conclusions: This case extends the longitudinal phenotypic characterization of DONSON-associated MISSLA and documents a distinct co-occurring variant configuration. The NMD result provides a testable transcript-level hypothesis for p.Arg442Ter, but the absence of parental phasing and patient-derived RNA or protein studies precludes definitive assignment of a patient-specific molecular mechanism.

title: Escaping cells dilute CRISPR screen responses unequally across cell types
abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens run in many cell types are used to compare how cell types respond to perturbation, to train models that transfer effects between them and to score such models. These uses assume that cells carrying a guide RNA had their target knocked down. Yet cells grow for days before sequencing: when an essential gene is knocked down, knocked-down cells are depleted or stop dividing while cells that escaped knockdown keep growing, and the measured response, an average over all cells carrying the guide, is diluted. We define the escape fraction of a perturbation as the share of its measured cells whose target was not effectively knocked down, and estimate it from each cell's counts of the targeted gene with a two-group mixture that recovers known fractions in simulated mixtures. In most cell types the escape fraction rises with how essential the gene is, it is higher in a later screen of the same cells, and it reaches about half of the measured cells in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). It predicts how much each response is diluted: the response size falls to (1 - e)^2 of that of the knocked-down cells. Because the escape fraction differs between cell types, it changes all three uses: hESCs respond like K562 cells unless knockdown depletes them, the coefficient a simple transfer model learns is lowered by the dilution of the cell type it predicts, and a benchmark scored on all cells rewards predictions shrunk towards no change, partly because that ground truth is itself diluted. Where cells stop dividing instead, the response also contains expression differences between cell-cycle stages. Response sizes should be compared on knocked-down cells or corrected for the escape fraction.

title: Synovial fluid glycosaminoglycans signature involved 3-O-sulfated heparan sulfate modulated by TGF-β pathway in OA
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) involved extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling of cartilage associated to inflammatory activation of fibroblastic like synoviocytes (FLS) from the synovium, but the molecular crosstalk between these two compartments remains poorly understood. Among Glycosaminoglycans (GAG) compound from ECM, heparan sulfate (HS) specifically regulate the bioavailability and activity of Heparin Binding Proteins (HBP), including cytokines and growth factors, such as TGF-{beta}, whose aberrant bioavailability in the synovial fluid (SF) could drive the catabolic process. Here, we investigated the composition, sulfation patterns and biological activities of GAG from OA SF that are currently uncharacterized and explored the regulation of 3-O-sulfated HS in TGF-{beta} mediated response in FLS. Total GAG from 52 OA-SF SF were extracted and quantitatively characterized by DMMB assay and HPLC. They are functional since they are able to bind several HBP with pleiotropic inflammatory and angiogenic properties according to ELISA competitive binding assay. They were able also to transactivate HBP signaling in cellular tests in-vitro, since they potentiated proliferative properties on fibroblastic and endothelial cells, and induced altered metabolic and inflammatory markers expressions in murine chondrocytes and human FLS. Although HS represented a minor fraction of SF-GAG, they contained a rare tri-sulfated disaccharidic fraction distinct from GAG from cartilage. Same GAG characterization was performed on FLS expanded from SF and SM samples. FLS exhibited also a rare sulfation pattern of 3-O-Sulfated HS on their surface analyzed by immunofluorescent staining, associated with the expression of 4 isoforms of 3-O-sulfotransferase (HS3ST) identified by RT-qPCR. TGF-{beta}1 treatment of FLS culture increases HS3ST expression profiles and HS sulfation pattern through the SMAD2/3 pathway, as observed by RT-qPCR, IF and western blot respectively. Finally, combined siRNA mediated silencing of these HS3ST enzymes affects FLS inflammatory secretome, according to proteome profiler cytokine arrays. among pro-inflammatory CXCL10 and CCL5 chemokines. Altogether, these data identify OA SF-GAG as new effective modulator of joint cell responses and reveal for the first time 3-O-sulfated HS and HS3ST patterns of expression in OA FLS associated with TGF-{beta}-Smad2/3-signaling pathway. Such specific HS fractions may contribute to the regulation of synovial inflammatory secretome, according to HBP partners that need to be further identified. However, this new glycanic mechanistic pathway sustaines the involvement of HS in OA progression and subsequently their interest as glycanic therapeutic targets.

title: Data Mining Sheds Light on a Novel Family of Plant-Associated Negative-Sense RNA Viruses Linked to Lispiviruses.
abstract: Large-scale mining of public transcriptomic datasets can reveal viral diversity that remains invisible to conventional virus-surveillance approaches, while increasingly powerful structure-prediction methods provide a complementary route to characterizing highly divergent viral proteins. Here, we combine sequence detection, phylogenetic analysis, structural prediction, and host-association analyses to investigate the cryptic diversity and biology of a new clade of plant-associated lispi-like viruses. Analyses of RNA-sequencing datasets identified and enabled assembly of 87 coding-complete lispi-like virus genome sequences associated with 75 plant hosts, expanding the known diversity of this new group by approximately 40-fold. The viruses share a conserved four-cistron genome organization, 3'-N(P1)-P2-P3-L(P4)-5', in which the first cistron is referred to interchangeably as N or P1 and the fourth as L or P4. Structural analyses generate testable structural hypotheses for the four conserved proteins. N (P1) adopts a canonical negative-strand RNA virus nucleocapsid architecture with conserved RNA-interacting residues and a predicted RNA-packaging configuration. P2 is exceptionally divergent, although a subset of structures resembles the ITPase/HAM1 fold. P3 forms a conserved trimeric coiled-coil architecture reminiscent of a viral fusion-protein stalk, but lacks the family-wide sequence features expected of a canonical membrane glycoprotein. L (P4) contains a structurally resolved Mononegavirales-type RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) core with invariant catalytic motifs, including the characteristic GDN signature, whereas its accessory regions are substantially more divergent. Phylogenetic insights form a distinct monophyletic lineage sister to the predominantly invertebrate-associated Lispiviridae, supporting their recognition as the new proposed family Masuviridae, comprising 15 tentative genera. Genus-level clustering is accompanied by marked differences in host association, ranging from strong specialization to broader host ranges. Retrospective screening of public sequencing libraries further identified lispi-like virus sequences in 1536 libraries representing 134 plant species, 11 plant families and 182 geographic locations, highlighting a substantial and geographically widespread cryptic virome. Together, these results establish Masuviridae as a deeply divergent lineage of plant-associated negative-sense RNA viruses and illustrate how the integration of sequence, structural, and large-scale transcriptomic analyses can move viral dark matter from detection towards evolutionary and functional characterization.

title: Deep-Learning-Assisted Integrated Microfluidic Platform for Automated Analysis of EV RNA Mutations.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry key genetic biomarkers, such as somatic mutations, making them valuable targets for non-invasive cancer diagnostics. However, standard workflows that isolate EVs and detect low-abundance mutations typically require multi-step manual operations, leading to sample loss and potential cross-contamination. Here, we present an integrated microfluidic platform combined with a deep learning algorithm for the continuous processing and automated droplet analysis of EV-derived RNA mutations. The microfluidic chip integrates magnetic bead-based EV capture, online lysis, droplet generation, and arrayed RT-droplet digital PCR (RT-ddPCR) on a single device. To streamline signal readout, a deep learning framework based on Cellpose and K-means clustering was implemented to process individual fluorescence images, enabling droplet detection, background removal, gray-scale intensity extraction, and automatic positive/negative droplet classification. The system showed a linear response across a wide range of original-sample inputs (R2 = 0.9950). The platform was evaluated using EV samples derived from three cancer cell lines (NCI-H1975, SK-LU-1, and HepG2) and the detection of EGFR L858R and KRAS mutations were achieved. By coupling continuous sample processing with automated image interpretation, this platform offers a practical reference for integrated EV nucleic acid analysis for liquid-biopsy applications.

title: Immunoinformatics-Guided Design, Immunological Evaluation, and Macrophage Transcriptomic Profiling of a Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis.
abstract: Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) causes Johne's disease in ruminants and is difficult to control once persistent infection is established. We designed a MAP multi-epitope vaccine candidate by screening conserved proteins and assembling predicted B-cell, MHC class I-restricted cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), and MHC class II-restricted helper T lymphocyte (HTL) epitopes into a recombinant construct. The construct was examined by physicochemical analysis, structural modeling, molecular docking, and immune simulation, then expressed in Escherichia coli and tested in BALB/c mice as a recombinant protein without external adjuvant or as an exploratory MYY-containing formulation, alongside PBS and inactivated-MAP controls.
